I think about this year the way I did last year and the years before. Nothing big has changed with my land, so why should I change much? My husband and the children help when they can, but two of them work in town, so I cannot do everything by hand. I hire a tractor for the heavy work.

My 60 mu — I split it like always. About 45 mu I plant wheat in autumn and then maize right after the wheat harvest in June. The other 15 mu I keep for cotton because my neighbor Old Wang has done cotton on that piece for years and it does well there. That land is a little sandier, better for cotton.

For the wheat: I always buy the improved seed from the agricultural supply shop in town — the man there sells what everyone in our village buys. Before planting I spread 2 bags of compound fertilizer per mu (the 15-15-15 kind, 50 jin bags, so 2 bags is 100 jin per mu). Then in spring when the wheat turns green I spread half a bag of urea per mu, maybe a little more if the leaves look yellow. I water the wheat — winter water before frost, then spring water, then one more when the heads are coming out, and one during the filling. Four waterings. I spray against the aphids and the rust maybe two or three times, whatever my neighbor is spraying I spray too.

For the maize after wheat — I use hybrid seed, the dealer recommends Zhengdan or something like that, everyone plants it. I spread 1 bag of compound and 1 bag of urea at planting, then top-dress another bag of urea at the big-trumpet stage when the plant is tall. I water two times if the rain is not enough. Spray once for the corn borer.

For cotton — I use the improved seed with the bollworm resistance, everyone does now. Cotton eats a lot of fertilizer and needs many sprayings. I put 2 bags compound as base, then urea at flowering and boll stage. Cotton I spray maybe 5 times, the aphids and bollworm never stop. I water 3 times.

I would rather put a little more fertilizer than too little. If I save 20 yuan on fertilizer and lose 100 jin of grain, that is a bad trade. The fertilizer is in the bag, I can see it — the yield is a hope.
